name: Babatana
confidence_why: The only description of Babatana itself, Whaley 1962, records a lexical contrast between long heavily stressed and short weakly stressed vowels but states that the analysis could not decide whether it is length or stress and gives no rule for where stress falls; Laycock 1982 merely doubts the length reading without offering a rule, and the penultimate-stress statement in Ross 2002 describes the neighbouring language Sisiqa, not Babatana.
catalog_citation: Whaley, Owen G. 1962. Babatana segmental phonemes. Te Reo 5: 60-62.
catalog_locator: p. 60, sec. 1.3 'Stress and Vowel Length'; word unit p. 60 sec. 1.4; orthography p. 62 sec. 3.1
catalog_quote: Phonetically long, heavily stressed vowels are in phonemic contrast with vowels which are short and weakly stressed. The analysis has not proceeded far enough for a phonemic interpretation of this contrast to be formulated solely in terms of short versus long, or stressed versus unstressed vowels. In the following examples vowel length is marked [:] and heavy stress [´]. [quru] "spear fish," [qú:ru] "pound nuts;" [tulu] "mute," [tú:lu] "three;" [mana] "past tense," [má:na] "blessing," [ká:kiti] "bite," [ká:kí:ti] "open up a boil;" [beré:] "how about you?", [bé:re] "laugh;" [kula] "dance," [kú:la] "elephantiasis." ... [sec. 3.1, p. 62] In the orthography used by Babatana at present, long or heavily stressed vowels are not marked.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (3 pp., CamScanner image PDF, no text; extracted text returns only form feeds) and rendered page 1 (= Te Reo 5 p. 60; page 2 carries the printed number '61.') to a PNG in the Section 1.3 'Stress and Vowel Length' is on page 1 and the quoted passage is there verbatim, including all six pairs [quru]/[qú:ru], [tulu]/[tú:lu], [mana]/[má:na], [ká:kiti]/[ká:kí:ti], [beré:]/[bé:re], [kula]/[kú:la]; the. mangles the acute accents ([ta:lul, [ki:lal etc.) but the report's quote follows the page scan, not the scanned. The section says only that long/heavily-stressed vowels contrast phonemically with short/weakly-stressed ones and that 'the analysis has not proceeded far enough' to decide whethe…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand statement on Babatana proper says that a heavy-stress-plus-length prominence is phonemically contrastive (minimal pairs where one member has a long, heavily stressed vowel and the other none, plus one positional pair beré: vs bé:re), but the author explicitly leaves open whether the contrast is one of length or of stress; no rule for the position of stress is given. Laycock 1982: 274 doubts the contrast and suggests it may follow from stress and/or open vs closed (underlyingly consonant-final) syllables. The nearest modern description, Ross 2002 on the sister variety Sisiqa (sisi1250), gives a penultimate default with secondary stress on the pre-antepenult and antepenult stress in echo-vowel words, which is what Laycock's suspicion would predict for Babatana; if that transfers, Babatana would read fixed: penultimate syllable on underlying forms, but no source states this for Babatana itself.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Whaley 1962. Ross 2002: 457 (Sisiqa, not Babatana) gives secondary stress on the pre-antepenult if any.
new_statements.exceptions: Whaley: none stated beyond the contrast itself. Ross 2002 (Sisiqa): reduplicated monosyllables take final stress (/zo'zo/ walk, /mi'mi/ see); certain tri- and tetrasyllables with identical last two vowels take antepenult stress (/'okene/ moon, /'ləgoto/ root, /mə'ləkana/ sky, /bə'lukuru/ wing), analysed as underlyingly consonant-final echo-vowel words.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolated citation forms elicited from one speaker (Esau Tuza) in phonetic transcription; Whaley defines the word as the 'minimal isolable utterance part'. Orthography does not mark the contrast (p. 62).
new_statements.identity_note: Whaley 1962 describes Babatana proper (informant Esau Tuza, Choiseul) = baba1268. The best modern description in the area, Ross 2002 'Sisiqa' (The Oceanic Languages 456-466, saved here), describes Sisiqa/Seqa (Senga, Sengga), which Glottolog codes as a separate language sisi1250, sister of baba1268 under East Choiseul (east2760); Tryon & Hackman 1983 and Ethnologue/Wikipedia treat it as a dialect of East Choiseul/Babatana, and Ross says its speakers are bilingual in Babatana with the differences eroding. For sisi1250 Ross 2002: 457 reads fixed: penultimate syllable (secondary on the pre-antepenult; final stress in reduplicated monosyllables; antepenult in echo-vowel words) — this is the statement the sisi1250 target (scan classification the named source could not be reached) was missing.
